video_notes.title: Communicate like McKinsey: top 3 consulting frameworks
video_notes.contributed: The core communication-of-insights framework in this cluster: know your goal / know your audience / know your approach, plus the Pyramid Principle, the Rule of Three, MECE, and the SCR (situation-complication-resolution) storytelling structure for high-stakes business communication.

video_notes.title: From LLM-as-a-Judge To Human-in-the-Loop: Rethinking Evaluation
video_notes.contributed: Shows how to communicate and validate the quality of a system's outputs to skeptical experts using pairwise LLM judging, an ELO ranking tournament, and a human-in-the-loop 'eyeballing' UI that surfaces the judge's qualitative explanation alongside the score.

video_notes.title: Design with AI - Full Guide (Tools, Workflows, Design Systems)
video_notes.contributed: Mostly a tool-selection guide for AI design workflows, not a communication framework, but it contributes concrete practices for presenting work-in-progress to stakeholders/clients cheaply (fast low-token demos before expensive high-fidelity ones), keeping documentation structurally consistent, and being able to narrate/justify a workflow or design decision in a review.

claims.claim: Flip the academic report structure (background then conclusion) into a business structure that leads with the answer, because executives care about the destination, not the breadcrumbs.
claims.quote: leading with an answer is the single biggest communication upgrade

claims.claim: Before any meeting, define what you need the audience to think, feel, and do by the end — not just what topic you'll cover.
claims.quote: what do you need the other person to think, to feel, and to do

claims.claim: Nearly every business communication goal is a flavor of three buckets: alignment (buy-in), education (bring someone up to speed), or problem-solving (decide together).
claims.quote: Alignment, education, and problem

claims.claim: A CEO is time-poor and outcome-driven — give them the answer first and evidence later, unlike a middle manager who needs structure or a junior analyst who needs more background.
claims.quote: time poor and outcomed driven

claims.claim: Always assume your audience has zero context on your topic, even after you've lived in the project for weeks, and open every meeting with a brief context-setting recap.
claims.quote: Always assume zero context.

claims.claim: Before presenting, identify the specific fears, concerns, and goals each stakeholder brings into the room so you can proactively address them.
claims.quote: their fears, their concerns, and their goals

claims.claim: Reframe a recommendation collaboratively (e.g. 'directing resources to the highest impact opportunities') instead of accusatorially (e.g. 'our current product isn't working') to avoid triggering defensiveness in stakeholders emotionally invested in the topic.
claims.quote: directing resources to the highest impact opportunities

claims.claim: Treat empathy in communication as a functional tool, not softness — it aligns your framing so you don't create unnecessary enemies while delivering the same message.
claims.quote: empathy in communication is a superpower

claims.claim: The Pyramid Principle, the dominant structure for business communication, was developed by Barbara Minto at McKinsey.
claims.quote: developed by Babrainto who was at Mckenzie

claims.claim: Structure any communication as a pyramid: the tip is your main message/recommendation/so-what, and the base is the supporting arguments and data.
claims.quote: your main message, your answer, your recommendation, your so what

claims.claim: Use the 'elevator with the CEO' test: if asked for a status update on the spot, give the direct recommendation and top risks immediately, not the research trail.
claims.quote: start with the answer first

claims.claim: Support your recommendation with exactly three arguments because the human brain is wired for three — it's the minimum for pattern recognition.
claims.quote: the human brain is wired for three

claims.claim: Three is also roughly the maximum number of points working memory can hold without overload — give someone seven arguments and they'll forget most of them by decision time.
claims.quote: maximum number for working memory without overload

claims.claim: Sequence supporting points deductively (major premise, minor premise, conclusion) when the audience is analytical and needs to follow logical proof.
claims.quote: major premise, minor premise and conclusion

claims.claim: Sequence points chronologically (step one, step two, step three) for a process, action plan, or roadmap — it's simple and easy to follow.
claims.quote: This is the natural time order sequence

claims.claim: Sequence points comparatively by degree of importance, leading with the strongest, so your key point lands even if the audience zones out later.
claims.quote: you start with your most important points

claims.claim: Build MECE (mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive) arguments — the three points must not overlap and together must form the complete picture, or someone can poke a hole in your case.
claims.quote: mutually exclusive, collectively exhaustive

claims.claim: For data-heavy presentations or skeptical audiences, use the SCR (situation-complication-resolution) framework to build the story before landing the recommendation, instead of leading with the answer.
claims.quote: situation complication and resolution

claims.claim: Open the situation section with non-controversial, already-agreed facts so the audience nods along and credibility is established before tension is introduced.
claims.quote: The situation component should not be surprising

claims.claim: The complication section introduces the problem, threat, or disruption, creating tension that makes the audience feel the recommendation is necessary or urgent.
claims.quote: This is where you introduce the problem or the tension

claims.claim: Deliver the resolution as a structured multi-part response (e.g. a three-part plan) so the recommendation feels earned rather than arbitrary.
claims.quote: we recommend a three-part response

claims.claim: Pairing SCR with the Pyramid Principle produces a communication that is both logically bulletproof and emotionally engaging.
claims.quote: logically bulletproof and is emotionally engaging

claims.claim: In a worked board-presentation example, the presenter opens by stating the alignment goal explicitly ('I need the board to say yes to a $2 million investment') and filters every slide and answer through that goal.
claims.quote: My goal in this meeting is alignment

claims.claim: Before any meeting, ask three questions: What is my goal? Who is my audience? What approach am I going to take?
claims.quote: What is my goal? Who is my audience? And what approach am I going to take?

claims.claim: Communication is a skill, not an innate talent — it improves with deliberate practice like any other skill.
claims.quote: Communication is not a talent that you are born with

claims.claim: Modern agentic RAG systems have so many tunable variations (retrieval pipeline, tool choice, agent architecture, model) that manually prototyping is easy but evaluating which variation is best is hard.
claims.quote: so many prompts that you can tweak

claims.claim: Handing 50-100 queries to a domain expert for manual review typically gets only one or two completed before the expert says they're too busy — a hard bottleneck for evaluation.
claims.quote: 50 to 100 queries to an expert

claims.claim: LLM judges scoring a single answer in isolation tend to be too optimistic and will find a tangential way to call the answer relevant, compared to human annotations.
claims.quote: LLMs are a bit too optimistic and they will kind of agree

claims.claim: Even though absolute LLM-judge scores are unreliable, sorting system variations from worst to best shows empirical agreement between the LLM judge and human experts on which system is worst and which is best.
claims.quote: the worst performing system is on the one on the left

claims.claim: Because LLMs are much better at distinguishing between a pair than scoring one answer, switch from single-answer scoring to pairwise comparison ('is A or B better').
claims.quote: should we then just ask the LM to compare two answers instead of one

claims.claim: Pairwise LLM judging is analogous to an eye exam: the judge just says 'left or right, which one is better' repeatedly rather than scoring in isolation.
claims.quote: Left or right? Which one is better?

claims.claim: Borrow the chess ELO ranking system to rank many RAG/agent variations: each variation is a 'player,' each query judged pairwise is a 'game,' and scores update based on expected vs actual outcome.
claims.quote: called the uh ELO ranking system

claims.claim: The open-source toolkit (referred to in transcript as 'write elo'/RAGElo) evaluates hit relevance per query, then judges which answer wins, and runs the ELO algorithm to produce a ranked list of systems.
claims.quote: developed this toolkit called write elo

claims.claim: A single pairwise win/loss verdict can hide nuance — e.g. the 'better' answer may just be more confident about an ambiguous term, when the actually-desired behavior might have been to ask a clarifying question back to the user.
claims.quote: winning is nuance right

claims.claim: Looking directly at individual query results ('eyeballing') via a search relevance workbench is a fast, concrete way to bring a human back into the evaluation loop rather than trusting the aggregate score alone.
claims.quote: eyeballing this gives us just a very easy way of looking at what is happening

claims.theme: Metrics can be text, not just numbers
claims.claim: A metric in an evaluation dashboard doesn't have to be a number — the judge's free-text explanation of why it picked a winner is itself a useful metric/label to surface to reviewers.
claims.quote: a metric could also be some text or a label that helps you understand something

claims.claim: Different agent/model configurations can retrieve wildly different numbers of hits for the same query (one config returned 111 hits) compared to older models that stop at 10 — a signal worth surfacing when comparing systems.
claims.quote: there are um 111 hits for this one

claims.claim: One model was observed 'cheating' by expanding a plain-language query into an exact-phrase search (quoted terms) to game retrieval — a failure mode that eyeballing surfaced but the standard scored dashboard did not.
claims.quote: GP5 mini will kind of cheat with the with the queries

claims.claim: Domain experts reviewing the underlying citations/hits alongside the generated answer can judge whether the citations actually make sense, not just whether the answer text sounds right.
claims.quote: subject matter expert who understands that domain you can look at that

claims.claim: A retrospective lesson: build evaluation tooling around n-number of experiment variants compared together, rather than pairwise experiments you have to awkwardly recombine yourself for 5+ systems.
claims.quote: n number of experiment variants within a single experiment

claims.claim: Rank-based overlap (RBO) and Jaccard similarity are good metrics for flagging which queries deserve human attention in ranked-list evaluation, but the same triage doesn't have a solved answer for long-form RAG answers.
claims.quote: very very good metrics for kind of uh sorting what queries

claims.claim: The team has not solved how to automatically signal that two long RAG answers are different enough (or in disagreement) to warrant human review.
claims.quote: how do you signal whether you need to look at these two answers

claims.claim: ELO ranking should not be computed as a simple average of per-query outcomes (0/1/2) — the current implementation does this, which the presenters flag as a modeling mismatch to fix.
claims.quote: ELO is not just the average of the per query

claims.claim: LLM judges cannot reproduce the same verdict every time on a rerun, but running many pairwise 'games' (as in chess ELO) partially compensates for this noise.
claims.quote: you cannot kind of reproduce the the the answers uh every time

claims.claim: Compared to 2022, when every word choice in a prompt could completely change an LLM's output, models today are noticeably more stable to prompt phrasing.
claims.quote: each word you put in the prompt might change the outcome completely

claims.claim: The same underlying model produces noticeably different output quality depending on which platform runs it — e.g. Grok's own platform beat the identical Grok model accessed through Cursor.
claims.quote: platform is not the same as model

claims.claim: In a head-to-head test generating the same dashboard, Grok took 2 minutes and 47,000 tokens for great quality, while Claude Fable took 17 minutes and 128,000 tokens for comparable quality.
claims.quote: took 2 minutes and 47,000 tokens with an great design quality

claims.claim: Use fast, low-token tools like Grok to produce a clickable live dashboard that can be screen-shared or deployed for an early client/stakeholder demo before investing in expensive high-fidelity generation.
claims.quote: deploy it to Verscell and share it with other people in my organization

claims.claim: Because a Grok-built prototype runs locally, you can share your screen and click through it live to talk through specific elements with team members, a stakeholder, or a client.
claims.quote: talk through specific elements with our team members, with a stakeholder, with a client

claims.claim: A rough AI-generated design that gets stakeholder buy-in on direction can still be rejected outright by executives with 'this is very off-brand' if it isn't reconnected to the real design system before that review.
claims.quote: this is very off-brand

claims.claim: When producing documentation for an audience (e.g. developers reading component docs), the top priority is consistency — every piece must share the same structure, or some readers get inconsistent, confusing information.
claims.quote: your priority here is consistency

claims.theme: Reusable structure beats ad hoc prompts
claims.claim: Building a defined 'skill' (a saved spec for what information must appear) produces consistent documentation on every run, versus ad hoc prompting a link and asking for 'documentation,' which yields different structure each time.
claims.quote: read the skill to understand the types of information that we want included

claims.claim: A dedicated accessibility-audit skill surfaced 22 issues (3 critical, 13 major, 6 minor) on one screen, deeper than a shallow generic chatbot check that would likely only flag the critical items.
claims.quote: it found 22 issues, three critical, 13 major, and six minor

claims.claim: Being able to narrate a multi-tool workflow (idea generation, prototyping, QA, then design-system alignment) in an interview or review is itself a way to demonstrate a senior, advanced process to a hiring manager or stakeholder.
claims.quote: you're already impressing the hiring manager

claims.theme: AI can't substitute for system-level understanding
claims.claim: AI cannot build a true design system end-to-end — it can produce styles, variables, or a button, but without someone who understands the rationale, no one can defend or explain the decisions in review.
claims.quote: The answer, no, it cannot

claims.theme: Can't explain what you didn't decide
claims.claim: If you can't answer 'when should this variant be used versus that one' about your own AI-generated tokens/components, you'll get pressed in a design review or by a developer and won't be able to defend the decision.
claims.quote: Do you know when surface subtle versus surface sunken should be applied

disagreements.topic: Whether to lead with the answer immediately or delay it to build a narrative

positions.position: The Pyramid Principle says always start with the answer first (the tip of the pyramid), then support it — this is presented as the default and 'the single biggest communication upgrade.'

The SCR framework says that for data-heavy presentations or skeptical audiences, you should build the situation and complication first and delay the recommendation/answer until the resolution, so it feels earned rather than arbitrary.

gaps: None of the three talks address how to design or format slides/visuals themselves (layout, typography, chart choice) for a presentation of insights — the McKinsey talk is about structuring the argument, not the deck.
The McKinsey talk doesn't cover how to handle live interruptions, hostile pushback, or being challenged mid-pyramid in the room beyond the single toothpaste framing example.
The McKinsey talk doesn't address remote/virtual presentation delivery (video calls, async written memos) versus in-person meetings.
The LLM-judge talk explicitly leaves open how to automatically detect when two long-form RAG answers are 'different enough' to need human review — stated as unsolved by the presenters themselves.
The LLM-judge talk doesn't discuss the cost or latency of running a full ELO tournament at scale (many systems x many queries x pairwise games), only that it works for their couple-week prototype.

The AI-design talk is fundamentally about tool selection and design-system workflows, not about communicating insights verbally or in writing — readers looking for data-storytelling or verbal delivery technique will not find it here.
None of the three talks discuss measuring whether a presentation of insights actually changed a decision or behavior after the meeting (follow-through/impact tracking).
